A Thermo-Elasto-Plastic Constitutive Model Based on Eulerian Strain Framework for wide-strain-rate response of polycrystals: Part Ⅰ Theory and Numerical Implementation
abstract: A thermo-elasto-plastic constitutive model for polycrystals is developed within an Eulerian strain framework, integrating the experimentally validated equation of state (EOS) with crystal plasticity theory, to characterize the wide-strain-rate response of crystalline materials under arbitrary dynamic high-pressure loading path. The EOS integration is founded on an Euler strain-based volumetric-deviatoric decoupling scheme, pivoting on the unique push-forward/pull-back operations between configurations for contravariant metric tensors. Integration of a statistics based mobile dislocation density model with a unified thermal activation – phonon drag dislocation motion model enables its broad strain-rate applicability, and the incorporation of both elastoplastic heating and viscous dissipation enhance its accuracy to capture dynamic temperature evolution. Furthermore, its predictive capacity for polycrystals and high-gradient deformations is enhanced by introducing grain boundary resistance and a recently developed slip-discreteness-corrected strain gradient crystal plasticity theory. Theoretical analyses and numerical simulations confirm the superior physical consistency and computational robustness of the Eulerian framework. The former is verified by comparing the analytic predictions of the Euler and Green schemes for different pure elastic large deformation scenarios, showing that traditional Green scheme tends to lose stability under large shear and uniaxial compression, whereas the Euler scheme predicts the evolution of stress, energy, and temperature with better physical consistency and numerical stability. The latter is validated through flyer-plate impact simulations, demonstrating the Euler scheme’s superior computational efficiency and numerical stability under extreme pressures. This Eulerian strain-based framework enables stable polycrystalline deformation calculations up to 200 GPa, while Green strain-based can only holds stability up to about 60 GPa. The model is capable of capturing the strain gradient effects caused by both inter-grain deformation inhomogeneity and sharp shock fronts. It reveals a unique strain-gradient-induced softening effect via local internal stresses from geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) at shock fronts, distinct from the hardening observed under quasi-static conditions. These advantages render it highly promising for engineering applications and facilitating systematic investigations of material responses under various dynamic high-pressure loading paths. In part II of this series, detailed simulations based on this model for shock and quasi-isentropic loading have been conducted to comprehend the path-dependent dynamic behavior and underlying mechanisms.

title: Phase transformation induced shear localization of metastable V10Cr10Fe48Co30Ni2 alloy: experiment and crystal plasticity simulation
Impact of ferrite/martensite interface on nanohardness in a Dual-Phase steel: A combined experimental and theoretical study
abstract: This combined experimental and theoretical study examines the impact of ferrite/martensite (F/M) interface on the hardness/indentation depth curve during nanoindentation tests on a Dual-Phase (DP) steel. Depth-dependent hardness measurements are performed and compared with the classical Indentation Size Effect (ISE), which typically predicts a monotonic decrease in hardness with increasing indentation depth. However, in ferritic regions near martensite, the present experimental investigation reveals a non-monotonic nanohardness behavior with an initial decrease due to the classic ISE, followed by an increase from a critical indentation depth and a final decrease from a second critical depth. The intermediate stage with an increase in nanohardness between these two critical depths indicates a localized hard- ening mechanism, which is not captured by the classic ISE model equation. Using a large enough dataset of representative indents performed in ferritic grains close to F/M interfaces, the experimental study demonstrates that this localized hardening is attributed to these specific interfaces acting as strong barriers to plasticity. It is also shown that the increase in nanohardness follows a clear power-law dependence on the microstructural surface geometric distance between the indent position and the nearby F/M interface location. A model, based on Strain Gradient Plasticity (SGP) theory, and explicitly accounting for this distance, is used to explain this nanohardness increase and estimate the evolutions of geometrically necessary dislocation (GND) densities between both critical indentation depths at the origin of the pronounced size-dependent strengthening. These results shed new light on the plasticity mechanisms that control hardness variations at the nanoscale in DP steels due to ferrite/martensite interface, and provide a framework for better understanding the effects of phase boundaries on localized plasticity.

title: A probabilistic model for dislocation channeling in irradiated FCC metals: the effects of stacking fault energy
Directed energy deposited SAF 3207/316L laminated stainless steel composite for enhanced hydrogen-embrittlement resistance and cryogenic tensile performance
Multiscale modeling of deformation and recrystallization in polycrystals using second-order self-consistent homogenization considering intragranular field fluctuations
An evolving non-associated Hill-Barlat yield criterion for anisotropic hardening with closed-form analytical calibration and guaranteed convexity
abstract: Accurate description of anisotropic hardening is critical for the predictive simulation of sheet metal forming. Within a non-associated flow rule framework, the evolving Hill48 family of models provides an attractive analytical route, in which the anisotropy parameters are obtained directly from the directional flow curves without optimization-based recalibration. Their quadratic structure, however, limits the curvature of the yield surface between the uniaxial and equibiaxial tension states. Higher curvature flexibility has been introduced through the coupled quadratic and non-quadratic (CQN) family, but the resulting yield functions require strain- and material-dependent verification of convexity, which can fail for realistic materials. This work proposes an evolving non-associated Hill48-Yld91 yield criterion that resolves both limitations. The Yld91 yield function controls the curvature through its non-quadratic exponent, while the quadratic Hill48 plastic potential captures the r -value anisotropy. Convexity is inherited intrinsically from the Yld91 structure, with no subsequent verification. The mathematical core of the work is an explicit closed-form analytical solution for the four Yld91 anisotropy parameters at exponent n =2, derived directly in terms of the Hill48 calibration coefficients, which reduces the evolving calibration to a single algebraic step without numerical iteration. By construction, the anisotropy parameters and the curvature-controlling exponent are obtained independently, so the deployment exponent can be chosen separately from the calibration. The proposed model is validated against the directional anisotropic hardening of two steels (718AT and MP980) and two aluminum alloys (AA5182-O and AA6022-T43), and is further tested for convexity against cases (QP1180 and an artificial material) for which CQN-type formulations have been reported to lose convexity. The framework provides a simple, analytically calibrated, and convexity-guaranteed route to evolving anisotropic hardening.

title: A hybrid approach to simulate the coupled thermo-viscoelasticity and damage of near-incompressible soft materials
Design and development of a wavy interlocking interface with a mineral–collagen fiber-like structure to enhance the strength of Al laminated alloys
A γ″ precipitate-evolution-informed CPFEM describing mechanical behavior of GH4169 under electropulsing-assisted aging
abstract: Electropulsing-assisted aging (EAA) has emerged as a promising route for modifying the microstructure and mechanical properties of thin-walled superalloy components. However, the relationships among current parameters, γ″ precipitate evolution, and mechanical response remain insufficiently understood. In this study, EAA and uniaxial tensile tests were performed on GH4169 sheet specimens. An electromigration-informed precipitate evolution model was established based on TEM observations, and a crystal plasticity finite element model (CPFEM) incorporating precipitate shearing and Orowan bypassing resistances was then developed, with a multi-phase representative volume element (RVE) model. The constitutive framework was implemented in Abaqus using VUMAT. Parameters were identified via inverse FE calibration with the particle swarm optimization (PSO) method. The results indicate a temperature-driven enhancement of electromigration during the γ″ coarsening process and a strengthening mechanism based on multi-mode shearing and bypassing. These findings provide a mechanistic basis for describing the EAA-modified tensile response of GH4169 and offer useful insight for future EAA-assisted processing of thin-walled superalloy components.

title: Non-admissible states in non-associated thermo-plasticity of hardening materials
abstract: Modeling plasticity under thermo-mechanical loading is of great interest in mechanical engineering. When constitutive equations were derived in the non-associated framework of Generalized Standard Materials, interpolation of material parameters as a function of temperature has been known for its lack of robustness, such as when the Armstrong--Frederick dynamic recovery parameter depends on temperature. In this work, excluding damage, the conditions under which unforeseen stages of stress softening occur are clarified, as well as are provided guidelines for robust thermo-plasticity of hardening materials. Non-admissible states for hardening elasto-plastic materials are defined as thermodynamics states with a strictly negative plastic modulus. Following this, a non-saturating kinematic hardening law is proposed for robust modeling of thermo-plasticity. It behaves asymptotically as a power-law at large plastic strain amplitude. One also designs a simple bi-isothermal test, first formulated as a thought experiment and then performed experimentally, to highlight spurious temperature-history effects with kinematic hardening modeling. This experiment reveals that the sign of the plastic modulus provides faithful insight about the robustness of the thermo-plastic hardening models. It is shown that the non-admissible states may exhibit problematic behaviors from non-zero initial values when the nonlinear kinematic hardening rule exhibits saturation, which is the case for most kinematic hardening laws. The proposed non-saturating law ensures a positive plastic modulus ---and positive intrinsic dissipation--- for any complex thermo-mechanical loading, thus forbidding non-admissible states and spurious stress softening for hardening materials.

title: Editorial Board
A coupled fully kinetic hydrogen transport and ductile phase-field fracture framework for modeling hydrogen embrittlement
abstract: Modeling hydrogen embrittlement (HE) is a long-standing engineering challenge, which has experienced significant developments in recent years. Yet, there is a gap in modeling the effect of the kinetics of hydrogen segregation at dislocations and the resulting interaction between ductile tearing and hydrogen-induced brittle fracture. In this work, a comprehensive chemo-mechanical framework is developed by coupling the fully kinetic hydrogen transport model with the geometric phase-field fracture method. A novel driving force is proposed that utilizes a hyperbolic tangent function of stress triaxiality to ensure that plastic dissipation contributes to fracture only under tensile conditions, phenomenologically representing void-driven ductile damage. The model successfully predicts the hydrogen-dependent shift in damage initiation from the specimen core to the surface. More importantly, hydrogen segregation at dislocations was shown to be crucial for modeling the multiple surface cracking experimentally observed at the necking region. Furthermore, the framework captures the competition between loading rates and diffusion kinetics, resolving the transition from multiple circumferential surface cracking at high strain rates to center-initiated single crack at lower rates. Finally, the model reproduced the experimental J-resistance curves for compact tension specimens, showing the transition from ductile tearing to embrittled crack.

A thermo-elasto-plastic constitutive model based on Eulerian strain framework for wide-strain-rate response of polycrystals: Part Ⅱ application for shock and quasi-isentropic loading
abstract: Leveraging the Eulerian strain-based polycrystalline thermo-elasto-plastic constitutive model developed in Part Ⅰ, this part systematically investigates the dynamic yield behaviors of LY12 alloy under shock and quasi-isentropic loading. The simulations replicate shock–reload/unload experiments by employing a multi-layered flyer with varying impact velocities, and using single-layered flyer with tailored ramp-loading-unload velocity profile to reproduce magnetically driven quasi-isentropic experiments. Yield strength is identified as the peak of the Von Mises flow stress under dynamic loading. Two peaks appear on each loading stage, one on the loading stage and another on the ensuing unloading or reloading stage; the first peak is persistently higher than the second one, therefore noted primary and secondary yield strength respectively. These findings settle the long-standing discrepancy that experiments using stress gauges always report yield stress higher than that by the self-consistent wave profile analysis, as the former actually detect the primary strength while the latter detect the second one. With increasing pressure, the primary strength shows a trend of quasi-linear increase followed by decrease under shock loading, while it exhibits a trend of monotonic quasi-linear increase under quasi-isentropic loading. The secondary strength follows a complex nonlinear zigzag trend of “increase, decrease, and increase again” under shock loading, but it holds the monotonic quasi-linear increase trend under quasi-isentropic loading. These path-dependent responses align well with available experiments. The drop of primary yielding in shock under higher pressures is revealed to be governed mainly by homogeneous dislocation nucleation, which is significantly intensified when the shock front is extremely narrowed under the condition of high-pressure shock loading with ultra-high local strain rate. The unique path-dependence of the secondary yield behavior is explained with the concept of critical dislocation density. This is the dislocation density at which the strength reaches the minimum during dislocation accumulation, increasing density before this point softens material, but hardens after it. The critical dislocation density is not a universal constant, but increases with the strain rate and temperature. Under shock loading, increasing pressure drives the dislocation density at the peak von Mises stress from below to far above the critical density. This transition causes the increase in dislocation density first to soften the material with increasing extent, then turn back even to hardening after reaching the maximum softening, upon increasing the shock pressure. The overall zigzag trend is thus manifested combining this trend with the monotonic strain-rate hardening. Whereas for quasi-isentropic loading, the peak dislocation density remains below the critical value, resulting in a monotonic trend. Yield response is also modulated by crystal orientation and strain gradients. Crystal orientation dictates the relative strength order: the primary yield strength under both loading paths follows the quasi-static trend, while the secondary strength order changes in the high-pressure regime of shock loading for their differences in forest hardening. Geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) soften the primary strength, but harden the secondary strength. title: Influence of stacking fault energy and slip planarity on dislocation/grain boundary interactions in FCC metals
abstract: The influence of stacking fault energy (SFE) and grain boundary geometric compatibility on the interactions between dislocations and grain boundaries in Ni, austenitic 316L stainless steel, and Al were studied using in situ high-resolution electron backscattered diffraction (HR-EBSD) and electron channeling contrast imaging (ECCI). The results show that the evolution of dislocation pileups is highly dependent on slip planarity, with localized stress fields forming in relatively low SFE materials such as Ni and 316L, while dislocation/grain boundary interactions in high SFE Al lead to the deformation of grain boundary structures and the early formation of sub-grain boundaries. Stress relaxation induced by dislocation/grain boundary interactions was only observed in Ni, while dislocations remained largely confined to discrete slip systems in 316L. The magnitude of the localized stress fields was found to be inversely correlated to the geometrical compatibility in the low SFE materials, but had no relation to the magnitude of stress concentration in Al. At increasing strain levels, the magnitude of local stress in the boundary vicinity was found to increase at the highest rate in 316L.

title: Understanding the role of hydrides in fatigue crack initiation behaviour in Ti-2Al-2.5Zr titanium alloy: Insights from quasi-in-situ fatigue tests and crystal plasticity methods
A stress-state-dependent secondary porosity model for impact failure in additive-manufactured metals and lattice architectures
Prediction of stacking fault energies and critical resolved shear stresses for hexagonal close-packed Mg solid solutions from first principle alloy theory
abstract: Stacking fault energies and critical resolved shear stresses (CRSSs) of different slip systems are predicted as a function of chemical composition for Mg solid solutions by accounting for chemical disorder, using the exact muffin-tin orbitals method involving coherent potential approximation and the semi-discrete variational Peierls–Nabarro model. A correlation between the stability of local atomic structure and stacking fault energies is established to understand the mechanisms behind the varied influences of alloying species. While addition of Ni, Co, Ti, and Ag (Sn, Ca, and Y) are demonstrated to significantly increase (decrease) the unstable stacking fault energy (γ us ) of prismatic and pyramidal 〈a〉 slip, Al, Li, and Zn yield relatively small influence. In addition, Sn, Ca, and Li decrease significantly both the intrinsic stacking fault energy (γ isf ) and γ us of pyramidal 〈c+a〉 slip. The varied influences of alloying species on stacking fault energies of prismatic/pyramidal 〈a〉 and pyramidal 〈c+a〉 slip are demonstrated to strongly correlate with the local structural stability of the body-centered orthorhombic and triclinic structure, respectively. The counterbalance between the influence of volume change and chemical composition on the local structural stability dominates the alloying effect on γ isf and γ us . Furthermore, the predicted dislocation core structure and CRSSs of both basal and non-basal slips based on the calculated stacking fault energies and elastic parameters are in line with the available experimental findings. Among the studied alloying species, addition of Ca, Li, Sn, and Y are found to significantly reduce the difference of CRSS between basal and non-basal slips of Mg alloys. The present advances provide a solid basis for understanding the atomic mechanisms of plastic deformation and intelligent design of high-performance Mg alloys.

Lath boundary spacing and orientation dominate damage and micro-/macro-shear banding in high-strength martensitic steel
abstract: Ultra-High Strength martensitic Steel (UHSS) often lacks the formability to undergo bending without cracking. We show that UHSS produced from heavily pancaked prior-austenite grains has a much lower bendability than UHSS from equiaxed prior-austenite, even though pancaked martensite has much more favorable habit plane orientations than equiaxed martensite, suggesting higher bendability through homogeneous deformation by in-habit-plane slip. Here, we analyze this contradiction using Electron Backscatter Diffraction (EBSD) - Scanning Electron Microscopy - Digital Image Correlation-based bending experiments. The tests yield microstructure-correlated strain maps, precisely aligned to EBSD-based (prior austenite) grain reconstructions, enabling pixelwise quantification of in-habit-plane versus out-of-habit-plane slip activity using the novel SSLIP framework. Besides plasticity, micro-damage is analyzed, revealing boundary cracking as the dominant micro-damage mechanism, most prevalent in pancaked martensite due to a combination of (1) fine auto-tempered martensite with high boundary density, originating from quenching deformed austenite, (2) habit plane orientations that only seem favorable (Schmid Factor > 0.3) but do not precisely match the optimal micro-shear band formation angle of 45°, and (3) a dense network of micro-shear bands. These micro-shear bands intersect with inter/intra-granular boundaries, resulting in micro-damage, and accelerated global macro-shear band formation and fracture. In contrast, equiaxed austenite results in coarser martensite laths, in which micro-shear bands form with fewer boundary intersections, resulting in localized plasticity without damage, explaining a 3–4 times better bendability despite a much stronger strain heterogeneity. Overall, the ability of UHSS to accommodate strain localizations without boundary cracking results in delayed global macro-shear band formation and increased formability, providing clear guidelines for further UHSS optimization through the size/shape of austenite, and resulting martensite lath orientation/coarseness.

title: Accurate characterization of circumferential uniaxial hardening and efficient modeling of biaxial hardening for anisotropic aluminum alloy tubes
A thermodynamically admissible fractional-order plasticity framework with state-dependent parameter learning for geomaterials
Fracturing in saturated porous media incorporating hydromechanical coupling and gravitational stress effect
abstract: The present work is devoted to numerical modeling of fracture initiation and propagation in saturated porous rocks. The emphasis is put on hydromechanical coupling and gravitational stress gradient effect. Compared with previous studies, several novel features are introduced. Based on the formulation of total potential energy and free poroelastic energy, the poroelastic relations of damaged porous media are established and the driving force of fracture propagation is identified. The effect of pore fluid pressure on fracturing is explored in greater depth by incorporating both effective stress and fluid enthalpy. Inspired by experimental results, the interaction between energy dissipation related to viscous fluid flow and fracture evolution is further investigated. Considering the strong pressure-dependency of mechanical behavior of rocks, the evolution of both tensile and shear fractures is influenced by compressive effective stresses. In order to better describe mixed fracturing in rocks under compression-dominating stresses, a hybrid phase-field model is proposed by considering two distinct driving forces respectively for tensile and shear fractures and their interaction is taken into account. Implemented in a finite element framework for fully coupled hydromechanical problems incorporating gravitational fluid flow and stress gradient, a wide series of representative cases are investigated. The proposed model is able to capture all main features involved in hydromechanical fracturing process. In particular, the kinetics of fracturing is influenced by fluid enthalpy contribution and pressure gradient. The proposed model is applied to investigate fracturing processes in laboratory tests under hypergravity conditions. The mechanistic mechanisms of hypergravity effect on fracturing pattern are elucidated.

title: Dislocation-climb-mediated void evolution in creeping metallic crystals
Cryogenic ultra-strong and ductile complex concentrated alloys achieved via non-equilibrium-solidification-enabled controlled recrystallization and multimodal precipitation
Nonlocal dislocation-density-based crystal plasticity simulation of the dislocation evolution in single crystal sapphire
abstract: With the growing demand for single-crystal and semiconductor materials, the design and control of defect-free single crystals have become a central focus in both research and industrial development. In this context, an established nonlocal dislocation-density-based crystal plasticity (CP) framework is extended and parameterized to simulate the evolution of dislocations in single-crystal sapphire during crystal growth and cooling. The model incorporates both mobile and dipole dislocation densities and accounts for their spatial transport, enabling an accurate description of dislocation generation, motion, and redistribution under large thermal gradients. The CP model is implemented within a thermo-mechanically coupled finite-element framework and validated against experimental measurements obtained from etched sapphire wafers. The simulations reproduce the measured dislocation-density trends and predict the formation of the characteristic dislocation pattern associated with the anisotropy of slip systems in sapphire. Using the validated model, optimized process parameters and furnace configurations are derived. The results show that a properly designed heating configuration combined with the derived growth and cooling rates can produce sapphire crystals with significantly reduced dislocation densities, minimal wafer deflection, and no cracking. The resulting nonlocal CP model thus provides a physically consistent and computationally efficient design tool for optimizing manufacturing processes in sapphire and other single-crystal semiconductors.

title: Sequential reorientation-to-twinning plasticity for sustained work hardening in high-strength dual-phase α′/α titanium alloys
Direct comparison of microstructurally small fatigue crack growth modeling: 3D mechanistic modeling compared with subsurface experiments
abstract: Microstructurally small fatigue cracks (MSFCs) challenge the predictions of classical linear elastic fracture mechanics (LEFM) due to significant microstructural influence on their growth directions, rates, and crack closure. This study integrates in-situ far-field high-energy diffraction microscopy and micro-computed tomography providing 3D, time-lapsed crack front characterization with direct comparisons to crystal plasticity finite element method (CPFEM) modeling on the exact same voxelized experimental IN718 microstructure. The accumulated plastic strain energy was employed as a metric to connect micromechanical fields to the crack extensions and growth rates. Pointwise comparisons along identical crack fronts at multiple fatigue stages quantify the accuracy of the CPFEM models developed across three different cycle counts in capturing experimental-derived stress fields, grain-scale crack path tortuosity, local crack growth rate variations, and crystallographic versus non-crystallographic transitions. Therefore, this comprehensive experimental dataset offers unparalleled opportunities for conducting a detailed, grain-by-grain comparison and corroboration for MSFC modeling for an additively manufactured IN718 material. This work advances MSFC modeling from a largely phenomenological basis, towards a physics-based, grain-resolved direct comparison between CPFEM and in-situ 3D experiments, from which mechanics-based modeling principles are extracted for dissipative energy driving force and local slip descriptors in order to inform microstructure-sensitive fatigue models.

title: An extended analytical model incorporating both elastic and chemical contributions for predicting solid solution strengthening in FCC multi-principal element alloys from 0 K to room temperature
Dislocation-mediated three-directional ε-lath network enabled excellent cryogenic strain hardening in a warm-rolled Fe49.8Mn30Co10Cr10C0.2 medium-entropy alloy
A strain-gradient elastoplastic model: Formulation, mixed finite element implementation and applications
abstract: A simplified strain-gradient elastoplastic model is developed within the framework of small-strain kinematics to describe size-dependent mechanical behaviour at the micro- and sub-micrometre scales. The formulation extends classical J 2 plasticity by incorporating both elastic and plastic strain gradients together with an intrinsic material length-scale parameter. Under elastic deformation, the conventional and higher-order stresses are derived from a strain-energy density containing quadratic contributions of the elastic strain gradients. Plastic flow is governed by a dissipation potential formulated in terms of the plastic strain rates and their gradients, leading to the emergence of higher-order (double) stresses while ensuring non-negative mechanical dissipation. The resulting constitutive equations are expressed in a unified non-incremental form, enabling active monotonic loading, partial or complete unloading, and subsequent reloading to be described without changing the governing equations. For efficient numerical implementation, the mixed finite-element formulation originally developed for strain-gradient elasticity – where displacement, strains, stresses, and their gradients are treated as independent variables – is extended to strain-gradient elastoplasticity. This extension reduces the continuity requirements to C⁰ finite elements and avoids higher-order interpolation. A multi-level Niterative procedure solves the resulting discrete nonlinear problem. The predictive capabilities of the proposed approach are demonstrated by analysing a notched plate subjected to uniaxial tension. The numerical results reveal pronounced size effects, including reduced notch opening, elevated stress levels near the notch tip, and a strong dependence on both the intrinsic material length scale and the notch geometry. The proposed framework captures the characteristic boundary-layer phenomena of strain-gradient plasticity, demonstrating that the developed mixed finite-element formulation provides an effective computational tool within the adopted small-strain framework.

title: Neural network-based distortional hardening inferred from experiments via FE-coupled backpropagation: Application to Ti-6Al-4V and third-generation AHSS
abstract: To learn the elasto-plastic constitutive response of metals from experiments with heterogeneous mechanical fields, we developed a finite element-coupled backpropagation algorithm that trains neural network-based plasticity models using force-displacement curves from notched tension and central-hole tension specimens. This approach enables training deep into the post-necking regime, well beyond the strain ranges accessible to standard uniaxial tests. Building on this framework, a neural network-based distortional hardening model is proposed in which a single network simultaneously predicts the flow resistance, anisotropic yield parameters, and yield function exponent of the YLD2000-3D yield locus as functions of equivalent plastic strain. This unified formulation enables continuous transition of the yield locus between sharp-cornered shapes and smooth shapes with high flexibility during deformation. The model is first pre-trained using uniaxial tension stress-strain data, after which the finite element-coupled training substantially improves predictions at large deformations. Ti-6Al-4V exhibits strong plastic anisotropy together with an unusual reversal in the orientation ranking of force-displacement responses between notched and central-hole tension specimens. The investigated third-generation advanced high-strength steel (AHSS) exhibits a hardening response that transitions from convex to concave curvature. For both materials, the proposed model accurately reproduces the large-deformation and post-necking behavior of all training experiments and successfully predicts unseen validation experiment results, including local strains and the evolution of Lankford coefficients. The proposed framework is computationally stable, efficient, and readily implementable in commercial finite element software. Moreover, the methodology is general and can be extended to arbitrary phenomenological yield functions and experimental training configurations.

title: Low-cycle fatigue life prediction of LPBF GH4169 via crystal plasticity: The dominant role of porosity defects
Plasticity driven elemental redistribution in microstructural evolution of multicomponent Ni-based superalloys: A thermodynamic-driven multicomponent crystal plasticity phase field modeling
Phenomenological-prior-based few-shot transfer learning for TA15 alloy constitutive modeling at high temperatures
A chemo–mechanical–damage framework with finite-rate hydrogen trapping: Geometry- and rate-controlled relevance of lattice–trap kinetics
Dual-mechanism plasticity for porous rocks: Development of a micromechanics-informed semi-analytical model
Cyclic plasticity constitutive modeling and microstructural mechanisms of AISI 304 stainless steel under random amplitude non-proportional loading
abstract: In practical engineering applications, key structural components are routinely subjected to complex non-proportional variable amplitude loading spectra that severely degrade the material’s fatigue life compared to the simple uniaxial conditions. The additional material response arising from the stochastic random loading significantly challenges the predictive efficacy of current cyclic plasticity constitutive model. To address this critical gap, the present study systematically investigates the cyclic deformation behaviors of AISI 304 stainless steel under constant amplitude, two-stage amplitude, and random amplitude fatigue loading conditions. A robust cyclic plasticity constitutive model is established, incorporating a dynamic plastic strain memory surface linked directly to evolving additional hardening response. Three non-proportional path parameters, comprising a newly proposed instantaneous factor and two classic history-dependent factors, are successfully integrated into a finite element analysis framework. The performance and predictive fidelity of each path factor are comprehensively quantified against experimental datasets. The newly proposed instantaneous path factor delivers the optimal predictive capacity, providing a precise boundary that closely tracks the multiaxial stress responses. Conversely, the history-dependent path factor proposed by Tanaka tends to be overly conservative by slightly overestimating the stress response, while the path factor proposed by Itoh et al. remains unconservative and underestimates the boundary. Furthermore, systematic transmission electron microscopy (TEM) observations reveal a clear physical correlation between macroscopic transient responses and their microstructural drivers. Loading paths with high non-proportionality culminate in the formation of refined dislocation cells or labyrinth substructures that act as formidable barriers to plastic flow. In contrast, the low non-proportionality path primarily exhibits oriented dislocation walls governed by a planar slip mechanism.

abstract: This work investigates the mechanics of plastic shock propagation and spall fracture in metal matrix composites. To this end, 53 planar plate impact experiments were conducted over an impact velocity range from 159.1 to 697.2 m/s on four SupremEX® material systems based on aerospace-grade aluminum alloys reinforced with ultrafine SiC particles---probing high strain rate conditions that have received limited attention for this class of advanced composites. The four materials span variations in heat treatment, reinforcement volume fraction, particle size, and matrix alloy, resulting in distinct influences on yield strength, tensile strength, and ductility. Photonic Doppler velocimetry was employed to measure the free surface velocity of the target, from which the shock velocity, shock stress, and spall strength were derived. These measurements were analysed within a Bayesian calibration framework, providing a statistically consistent inference of shock and spall properties across the different material systems, while accounting for experimental uncertainty and specimen-to-specimen variability in the mechanical response. To the authors' knowledge, this work constitutes the first application of a Bayesian inference framework to the combined analysis of shock and spall data from plate impact experiments in metal matrix composites, establishing a rigorous basis for probabilistic comparison of material responses and for uncertainty-aware modeling of dynamic failure. In addition, the specimens were soft-recovered and examined by scanning electron microscopy and X-ray tomography. The investigated impact velocities span the transition from incipient spall, characterized by discontinuous cracking and limited void growth, to spallation-induced specimen fragmentation. X-ray tomography provided three-dimensional reconstructions of the spall morphology, yielding quantitative information on the evolution of fracture size and volume with increasing impact velocity. Scanning electron microscopy revealed characteristic damage features associated with spallation—including void growth and coalescence, intervoid cracking, particle/matrix debonding, and localized particle fracture—and showed that fracture morphology varies among the composite systems, reflecting the influence of reinforcement architecture on damage evolution. Together, these observations establish a direct connection between microstructural damage evolution and the macroscopic shock and spall response of the four advanced metal matrix composite systems under the investigated loading conditions.

A unified multi-scale machine learning accelerated homogenization theory for anisotropic elastoplasticity and progressive damage up to failure in highly aligned graphene-Cu nanocomposites
abstract: Unlike the isotropic elastoplastic behaviors of randomly distributed nanocomposites, the anisotropic mechanical lifespans of highly aligned graphene-based nanocomposites remain unexplored under realistic configurations. In this paper, a unified multi-scale machine learning accelerated homogenization theory is established for anisotropic elastoplasticity and progressive damage up to failure in highly aligned graphene/Cu nanocomposites. First, an upscaling MT 2 -FE framework is proposed by integrating the dual-scale micromechanics-based representative volume element homogenization (MT 2 ) with macroscopic finite element (FE) simulation. Progressive interfacial degradation is illustrated by the load transfer and interfacial contact. The orientation-dependent progressive damage of the Cu matrix is characterized by the irreversible thermodynamics with tensor-form field-fluctuation method. Subsequently, an anisotropic micromechanics-driven recurrent neural network (RNN) surrogate model is trained on datasets generated by the dual-scale MT 2 model under non-monotonic loading paths to formulate the accelerated RNN-FE scheme. The anisotropic lifespans of highly aligned graphene/Cu nanocomposites are experimentally validated along both in-plane and out-of-plane directions. The accelerated RNN-FE scheme accurately captures these anisotropic and path-dependent mechanical responses while remarkably reducing the online computational time of proposed MT 2 -FE framework by 99%. The aligned arrangement of graphenes is demonstrated to delay the damage initiation under in-plane loadings, albeit at the expense of out-of-plane mechanical performance. This paper provides the design guidance for microstructure and macroscopic configuration of highly aligned graphene-based nanocomposites.

Using instrumented indentation to identify site-specific deformation mechanisms in polycrystalline Mg-Y alloys
abstract: Abstract The active slip systems and strain hardening in Mg-1wt.% (0.28 at.%) Y were investigated using instrumented indentation. Spherical indentation was employed to estimate the stress-strain response of individual grains, while Berkovich indentation was conducted at different strain rates to investigate the active deformation modes. Slip trace analysis indicates that pyramidal slip system is activated in all grains tested over a wide range of grain orientations (characterized by misorientation angle between indentation axis and hcp c-axis). With increasing indentation strain rate, an increase in hardness was observed, accompanied by enhanced basal slip activity. Indentation at grain boundaries revealed misalignment between slip traces in the grain boundary regions and those within the adjacent grain interiors. These results indicate that pyramidal < c + a > slip in dilute Mg-Y alloys can be activated in the center of grains and is not caused by grain boundaries.

title: Cementite-lamella morphology and inter-nodule compatibility govern hierarchical plasticity in pearlitic steel
Micromechanics-informed coupled viscoplastic–damage model for voided composites with non-associated flow and lode-angle dependence
abstract: The plastic flow direction in voided particulate composites does not coincide with the outward normal to the yield surface, a deviation quantified here at a mean angular error of 23.3° across 1,001 multiaxial micromechanical stress states — establishing that non-associated flow is a physically necessary and micromechanically verifiable feature of this material class. A micromechanics-informed, fully coupled viscoplastic–damage constitutive model is developed in which the yield surface — closed in the hydrostatic direction, Lode-angle dependent, and verified convex over the full calibration domain, along with the plastic potential and hardening law, are each derived from multiaxial micromechanical homogenization data rather than postulated or fitted to macroscopic experiments; the coupled evolution laws are shown to satisfy the dissipation inequality over the admissible stress domain, establishing thermodynamic admissibility. A single invariant-based criterion governs both compression-dominated viscoplastic flow and tension-dominated brittle damage through a crack-band regularized Rankine criterion, allowing regime transitions without separate criteria. The framework is implemented as an open-source user-material subroutine for Abaqus/Explicit and validated against quasi-static and dynamic experiments across three orders of magnitude in strain rate. Peak-force predictions agree with the quasi-static and dynamic experiments to within 3.0% and 1.1%, respectively, and the model reproduces without recalibration the experimentally observed 27% increase in peak force from quasi-static to dynamic loading. Although calibrated for a specific grade, the constitutive structure is grade-agnostic and directly extensible to the broader class of voided particulate composites and porous resin systems. The user-material is provided as supplementary material.

title: Microstructural influences on low-temperature grain-scale deformation behavior in an Fe-Ni alloy
abstract: Three-dimensional high-energy X-ray diffraction microscopy (HEDM) was performed in situ on Fe-36Ni Invar samples as they were plastically deformed at room temperature and at -55 °C. Statistical correlation analyses were performed on local and neighborhood microstructural and micromechanical descriptors with grain-averaged stress and diffraction peak broadening (plasticity) metrics as applied strain was increased. For the room temperature sample, 1430 grains were analyzed while for the low-temperature sample, 1407 grains were analyzed. Analyses of grains and neighborhoods revealed that local grain micromechanical descriptors play a dominant role in determining grain stresses while grain geometry predominates the microscale development of plasticity. Further, it was found that, as temperature decreased, the influence of neighborhood on grain deformation response increased. In addition, surface grains were found to be more influenced by their neighborhood than embedded grains.

abstract: Quenching and partitioning (Q&P) steels deform through coupled crystallographic slip, retained austenite transformation, heat generation, and progressive degradation. This work presents a thermomechanically coupled crystal plasticity damage model within a modified Taylor homogenization framework. The main extension is a bounded, phase sensitive effective damage variable that combines ferrite matrix damage with ferrite–martensite and austenite–containing interface degradation while retaining explicit coupling to martensitic transformation and temperature evolution. The framework is calibrated and assessed using tensile, retained-austenite, and thermal data for QP3Mn and QP980 steels. For QP3Mn, the model captures the stress response and retained-austenite depletion under different strain rate and temperature conditions. For QP980, it captures the rate-dependent tensile response and internal temperature evolution. Model assessment is restricted to the uniform deformation regime up to the maximum load point; the subsequent response is interpreted as constitutive degradation rather than a prediction of necking, crack propagation, or fracture morphology. The simulations distinguish the maximum load point from the subsequent acceleration of degradation and the transformation-damage crossover. The results show that retained-austenite transformation stabilizes deformation when it remains active over the strain interval preceding maximum load, whereas early exhaustion of transformation promotes an earlier transition to degradation-dominated response.

title: A first experiment at interfacing crystal plasticity and continuum dislocation dynamics

Distinct structural and energetic origins of {101‾1} compression twinning in HCP metals
abstract: Combined theoretical-experimental research has been undertaken on deformation twinning in hcp-Ti and to resolve key factors that contribute to CRSS evaluation. We analyze one of the most challenging cases of { 10 1 ¯ 1 } twin in Ti to establish its coherent boundary structure, the operative twin-dislocation layers that mediate its growth, and the associated energetics. In particular, the discrete lattice offsets defining the coherent twin boundary structure cannot be assumed a-priori, since an incorrect boundary structure leads directly to erroneous twin boundary energies. Furthermore, although multiple shear-shuffle combinations are crystallographically admissible for twin growth, the minimum-energy pathway (MEP) has not been determined. The required atomic shuffles vary from layer to layer and exhibit complex three-dimensional patterns, making a rigorous atomistic treatment essential for accurate barrier calculations. Within a density functional theory framework, the two experimentally observed twinning dislocations, b 2 and b 4 (associated with two- and four-layer twin-boundary migration, respectively) are systematically considered and reveal that the b 2 mechanism is energetically preferred and governs twin progression. The DFT calculations combined with the nudge elastic band (NEB) algorithm show that { 10 1 ¯ 1 } exhibit unusually high unstable fault energies ( γ ut ) , a low twin boundary energy ( γ tsf ) with a high twin boundary migration resistance ( γ T B M ) arising from the exceptionally large atomic shuffles. Extending the simulations to room temperature through ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD), a simple twin model predicts a twinning stress (CRSS) of approximately 370 MPa for Ti, in agreement with experiment. To validate the theory, unique in situ TEM loading experiments were designed to activate { 10 1 ¯ 1 } twin on carefully oriented samples of Ti with measurements of load-displacement response, electron diffraction, and lattice reorientation are all consistent with the theory. A comparative study across Zr, Hf, Mg, Zn, and Be confirms the distinctive { 10 1 ¯ 1 } Ti trends and reveals the corresponding CRSS characteristics among other HCP metals.

Crystal plasticity analysis of dissipation under low-amplitude cyclic loading: from slip-band activation to self-heating curves
abstract: Dissipation analysis under low-amplitude cyclic loading, commonly referred to as self-heating measurements, is an increasingly used experimental method for estimating high-cycle fatigue (HCF) properties. While a two-scale probabilistic model (Poisson point process, PPP) successfully links self-heating curves to HCF scatter, the physical nature of the postulated plastic activation sites has never been examined through full-field polycrystalline simulations. This work addresses this gap by introducing an explicit lamellar representation of slip bands within individual grains of a polycrystalline representative volume element, combining FFT-based crystal plasticity with grain-scale variability of the critical resolved shear stress. This lamella-scale framework captures the heterogeneous and progressive onset of microplasticity under uniaxial cyclic loading (R = −1). The main results are threefold: (i) the number of plastically active lamellae follows a power-law distribution in stress amplitude, in quantitative agreement with the PPP hypothesis; (ii) the mean steady-state dissipation per cycle reproduces the secondary regime of experimental self-heating curves; (iii) a fatigue indicator parameter (FIP) based on cumulative plastic slip at the lamella scale exhibits a Weibull-type scatter whose shape parameter is consistent with experimental HCF variability. These results provide a microstructural justification for the assumptions of the two-scale probabilistic model and establish a physically grounded connection between slip-band activation, self-heating measurements, and HCF scatter.

title: Understanding the effect of neutron dose on plastic deformation, fracture nucleation, and toughness using a crystal plasticity phase field fracture model and a microscale J-integral methodology
abstract: Predicting neutron irradiation embrittlement in reactor pressure vessel (RPV) steels requires understanding three microscale interplays that remain poorly resolved: the coupling between irradiation-induced plasticity and fracture, the distinct roles of fracture nucleation versus propagation, and the influence of irradiation hardening on measurable fracture toughness. To resolve these, a unified computational framework was developed for JRQ ferritic RPV steel coupling crystal plasticity finite element (CPFE) modelling with phase field fracture. Regarding plasticity–fracture coupling, a dislocation-based deformation model incorporating dose-dependent hardening from dislocation loops and solute clusters, calibrated against tensile data up to 1.04 dpa and validated against microscopic digital image correlation for unirradiated material, was directly coupled to the fracture formulation; irradiation hardening was found to reduce fracture toughness, though not to the extent observed experimentally, confirming that plasticity is a necessary but insufficient descriptor of the ductile to brittle transition. Regarding nucleation and propagation, fracture nucleation and propagation are typically conflated in mesoscale models; by assigning separate phase field parameters to each regime, independent calibration becomes possible, enabling the contribution of each stage to be isolated and quantified. Regarding fracture toughness evaluation, J-integral contours computed around predefined cracks in the CPFE model were validated against energy release rates from force–displacement curves in both elastic and elastic–plastic regimes, yielding path-independent results; microstructural heterogeneity increased J-values by only 5.71% relative to a homogeneous model. The framework establishes a mesoscale bridge between grain-scale deformation mechanisms and the macroscopic fracture behaviour transition of irradiated RPV steels.

title: Comparison of phase field formulations to capture dislocation interactions within elastically inhomogeneous media
An integrative multi-fidelity framework for fatigue life prediction in additively manufactured 316L stainless steel
abstract: This study develops a multi-fidelity framework for assessing fatigue-critical environments and fatigue life in laser powder bed fusion 316L stainless steel under optimized, lack-of-fusion, and keyholing process conditions. X-ray computed tomography provides three-dimensional pore morphology and positions. A melt-pool-informed generator creates process-dependent three-dimensional synthetic grain fields, assigning regional morphology and texture across core, boundary, and transition regions. Using scan parameters and calculated melt-pool geometry, the generator calibrates grain morphology and texture against electron backscatter diffraction descriptors. Crystal elasticity simulations of cropped subvolumes screen and rank candidate fatigue-critical environments, after which hotspot-centered crystal plasticity finite element simulations resolve stabilized local cyclic strain. The resulting local strain corrections are applied to a strain–life relation calibrated to the optimized process condition using an imposed initial stress-free reference state. The modeled candidate environments are qualitatively consistent with the defect classes and surface proximity of fracture origins identified by post-mortem fractography. For representative specimens from the three process conditions, the fatigue-life predictions follow the measured ordering and differ from the measured lives by less than 15%. Controlled sensitivity studies show that spherical idealization of the examined lack-of-fusion pores changes the estimated life more than volume-equivalent ellipsoidal idealization does. For the tested statistical inputs, the estimated life is more sensitive to the prescribed upper-tail grain-size target than to the assigned crystallographic texture. Three synthetic realizations produce a reconstruction-related full range in estimated life equal to 7.6% of their mean. The framework quantifies sensitivity to XCT-resolved porosity and melt-pool-informed statistical crystallographic inputs within the modeled scope.

Mechanistic differences between hydrogen-related intergranular and transgranular fractures in tempered martensitic steel revealed by frozen-in hydrogen distribution
abstract: Intergranular (IG) and transgranular (TG) fractures, which often occur in the elastic and plastic regions in tensile tests, respectively, are observed in hydrogen embrittlement of tempered martensitic steels. In the present study, a frozen-in hydrogen distribution technique was applied to investigate the elementary processes preceding hydrogen-related TG fracture. The elementary processes between IG and TG fractures were compared in terms of hydrogen redistribution and the interaction of hydrogen with lattice defects during elastic and plastic deformation. Tensile testing with frozen-in hydrogen distributions and thermal desorption analysis before and after stress preloading showed that plastic deformation in the presence of hydrogen leaves a persistent state affecting subsequent ductility and TG fracture behavior. The combined results are consistent with the formation of a persistent hydrogen-defect state inside prior austenite grains (PAGs). One possible interpretation is that plasticity-induced trapping sites, potentially including dislocations and vacancy-type defects, compete with prior austenite grain boundaries (PAGBs) for diffusible hydrogen. These sites may trap hydrogen diffusing toward PAGBs and hydrogen temporarily detrapped from PAGBs, thereby suppressing a further increase in hydrogen content on PAGBs while increasing that inside PAGs. This possible hydrogen redistribution, together with the accumulation of vacancy-type defects inside PAGs, may contribute to the relative promotion of TG fracture. These findings suggest that the dominant elementary processes differ between TG fracture in the plastic region and IG fracture in the elastic region, the latter being governed primarily by hydrogen accumulation on PAGBs through stress-induced diffusion.

title: A dislocation-mediated multi-phase-field model for coupled evolution of precipitates, voids and cracks during creep of Ni-based single crystal superalloys
A Generalized Crystal Plasticity Framework for Reversible and Irreversible Slip in FCC Metals
abstract: Dislocation glide is the fundamental mechanism of crystal plasticity. Atomistic simulations and in situ experimental observations have provided direct evidence that dislocation motion is reversible under small deformation, size confinement, and weak dislocation interactions. Classical crystal plasticity generally treats slip as an irreversible process and therefore cannot describe this mechanism. In this work, we develop a generalized crystal plasticity model for FCC metals that accounts for both the reversible and irreversible parts of plastic deformation. For the reversible part, the model describes plastic reversal through two mechanisms: dislocation backtracking along the original slip path and reversible decoupling of slip system interactions. For the irreversible part, the model represents the capture of mobile dislocations by dislocation entanglements, which retains the forward slip history as stable defect structures. Therefore, under large deformation, larger sample size, or strong dislocation interactions, the plastic deformation and dislocation evolution predicted by the generalized model follow cumulative features consistent with classical crystal plasticity. A variational framework with conservative and viscous potentials derives the microforce balance for reversible slip evolution, incorporating phonon drag, thermal activation, stored energy, and forest hardening. The model is implemented in finite elements and applied to single crystals, bicrystals, and polycrystals. For Al under [123] single slip, the model captures nonlinear unloading, with the reversible plastic fraction decreasing as the maximum strain increases. Under [012] double slip, Hirth lock formation during forward loading restricts reverse motion, leaving larger residual strain. For an Au bicrystal, the predicted pseudoelastic response matches experimental measurements, which highlights the role of grain boundaries in regulating slip backtracking. Polycrystalline Al simulations predict that fine grains promote plastic reversal by restricting the glide distance available for mobile dislocations to interact with forest obstacles and form stable junctions or lock structures. Lower initial forest dislocation density increases reversibility and reduces stored defect energy, delaying damage initiation. The model provides a physically based framework for predicting reversible plasticity in FCC metals and guides design of nanometallic materials with high damage tolerance and reversible energy storage.

title: Anisotropic inelasticity in two-dimensional network glasses
abstract: We systematically investigate the orientation-dependent mechanical response of two-dimensional network glasses subjected to area-preserving pure-shear deformation at different loading angles. While the small-strain elastic response is nearly isotropic, the finite-deformation regime preceding failure exhibits pronounced nonlinear and orientation-dependent behavior, including non-coaxiality between the principal stress and strain axes. The inelastic response reveals an anisotropic failure landscape governed by the degree of structural disorder. Increasing heterogeneity reduces the overall strength and progressively suppresses directional dependence, resulting in a more isotropic failure response. At larger strains, irreversible bond rupture causes a loss of tensile load-bearing capacity and pronounced strain softening of the major principal stress. In contrast, the principal shear stress remains relatively stable as the network undergoes local rearrangements that continue to sustain compressive load transfer. The results demonstrate that both the magnitude and character of anisotropy evolve dynamically throughout deformation. At intermediate strains, the anisotropic response is primarily governed by intrinsic structural symmetries, whereas at larger strains it becomes dominated by the evolving spatial distribution of damage.
